job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Yusuf Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work as a junior loan analyst at Calder Building Society in Manchester, started in September. Most days I check mortgage applications: pay slips, credit files, whether the numbers hang together. I share a three-bed with two friends from uni, and we split a slow cooker lasagne most Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what drags?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the moments when a file is messy and I have to work out the story behind it, like a couple whose income changed halfway through the year. The drag is the pile of ticking boxes before I get to that. My mum's a nurse and a union rep, and she's backing me with a bit of a safety net, so money isn't the stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world wasn't ready for the wild version anyway. At work I'd tell the team the tools are helpful for first drafts and nothing more. Online I'd just share something sensible and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means more of the same, which suits me while I'm learning. My seniors keep the judgement, and I'd get a bit quicker at the routine checks. I have over six months saved, and there are plenty of building societies and banks hiring in Manchester, so I feel pretty steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the job and pass the first mortgage-advice exam this spring. I'd use the AI tool on my phone a bit more for plain-English summaries of lending rules. And I'd keep putting £300 a month in a savings account for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the version of the future where I can get on with being twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly summarising long policy documents and drafting polite emails to customers who sent the wrong paperwork. It saves me maybe twenty minutes a day. I always check it against the actual policy, because once it gave me a rule from a different lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the thing that might still catch you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent. My flatmate Adam's lease is up in the summer and the landlord could put it up by a lot. That, and my team could get slashed anyway in a bad year for housing, nothing to do with AI. I'd still be fine, but it's the thing on my mind.

say: I'd say the **hype** was overblown but the tools are fine for first drafts.
I'd tell the team to keep using AI for **summaries**, with a human check.
think: I think this means **more of the same**, and my seniors keep the judgement.
My money and local **openings** make me feel steady.
do: Pass the first mortgage-advice **exam** this spring.
Use my phone's AI tool for plain-English **summaries** of lending rules.
Put **£300 a month** into a deposit account.
feel: I feel **calm**, like I can get on with being twenty-two.
S0.quote: I always check it against the actual policy, because once it gave me a rule from a different lender.
fieldNote: Yusuf is **secure**, with savings, openings nearby and a job he's learning.
He uses AI **sparingly** and checks it, a habit he picked up from one mistake.
His only worry in the mild case is **rent**, not technology.

steps.text: Pass the first mortgage-advice exam this spring
Use the AI tool to summarise lending rules, then check them
Put £300 a month into a deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving quickly and we should be honest about it. At work I'd say the society should pair the new tools with real training, not just cuts. I'd probably bring it up at our staff forum, because my mum taught me to speak up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the first-pass checks I do are exactly what gets automated. A loan file goes in, the system reads the pay slip, flags oddities and a senior signs off. That might leave a quarter of the team doing what ten used to. I'd be near the bottom of the list, being the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it by learning the tool properly, not just using it now and then. I'd ask to sit with the underwriters, since that's the judgement end, and move toward it. I'd also step the deposit saving up to £450 a month, because I'd rather have the cushion than the lasagne nights out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared stiff. It's a bit like starting a game where the rules got rewritten after the first level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Checking is your daily job. Which parts of it would go first at Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine checks: matching pay slips to bank statements, reading credit files, filling in the standard form. The conversations with customers who've got a strange story would stay, because those need a person. So my best bet is to become the person who handles the strange ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you talk about this with your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say get the union involved early. She's seen the same thing at the hospital with new systems, and she says the staff who spoke up got retraining and the ones who stayed quiet got moved. I'd tell her I'm already on it, then she'd tell me to take notes.

say: I'd say the society should pair new tools with real **training**, not just cuts.
I'd raise it at the **staff forum**, as my mum taught me.
think: I think the **first-pass checks** I do are exactly what gets automated.
As the newest person, I'd be **near the bottom** of the list.
do: Learn the tool **properly** and ask to sit with the underwriters.
Raise my deposit saving to **£450** a month.
Take **notes** at the staff forum and join the union.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but not scared stiff, like the rules were rewritten after level one.
S1.quote: The conversations with customers who've got a strange story would stay, because those need a person.
fieldNote: Yusuf targets **judgement work** as his route, a classic move for an early-career analyst.
His mother's **union** habit shapes his instinct to speak up early.
He labels himself uneasy, but his own team's size could shrink, so **anxious** fits.

steps.text: Learn the loan-checking tool properly, beyond summaries
Ask the underwriters if I can sit with them weekly
Raise deposit saving to £450 a month
Join the union and speak up at the staff forum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments, firms and unions need to get in a room this month. I'd push for a guaranteed income and a stake for workers in what AI produces. I'd say it as plainly as I can, because there's no time for a long argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone, and probably most office finance jobs along with it. A loan analyst is thinking work by definition. I'd be twenty-four, with some savings and no qualifications anyone will pay for. Robots for hands-on work come three years after, which doesn't help me because I've never worked with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, because it's good money while it lasts, and bank as much as I can, maybe £600 a month. I'd ask my mum if I could move back home for a bit to save rent. And I'd look at jobs that need a person in the room, like financial advice for older people, or working for a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I think my body would be tense all the time. I'd also feel angry that nobody asked ordinary people whether we wanted this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years leaves very little. What changes first in how you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the takeaways and the subscriptions, and probably let my flatmate know I might leave early. The first week I'd phone my mum and my dad and tell them straight. I'd be afraid, but I'd also be curious about what the new world looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the society offered a redundancy package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, if the money was decent, and I'd use it as a bridge. A redundancy package gives me a few months to retrain without panicking. I'd say sorry to my team, though, because they're friends and I'd feel like I'm leaving them to carry it.

say: I'd say governments, firms and unions must meet and agree a **guaranteed income**.
I'd push for workers to get a **stake** in what AI produces.
think: Privately, I think my **job** is gone, along with most office finance jobs.
Robots arrive later, but I've never worked with my **hands**, so no extra time.
do: Keep working and bank about **£600 a month** while it lasts.
Ask my mum if I can move **home** to save rent.
Look at **person-to-person** jobs like advice for older people.
feel: I feel **heavy** and tense, and angry that ordinary people weren't asked.
S2.quote: A redundancy package gives me a few months to retrain without panicking.
fieldNote: Yusuf **expects** his job to go and says so plainly, even with six months saved.
He turns to **family** and a bridge plan quickly.
Anger at who decided is **political**, not personal.

steps.text: Bank £600 a month while the job lasts
Ask my mum about moving home to save rent
Look for advice work with older customers
Push for a guaranteed income through the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window, so let's use it for retraining and fair rules. I'd say that to colleagues and probably on my local forum. It's a chance to shape things, not just to complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get about five working years, long enough to build a real base. By then I'd be twenty-seven and a senior analyst on paper. But I'd also know that anything I'm good at, a machine will be better at by 2031, so I'd treat the next years as preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams, then use my work time to learn AI properly. I'd save about 40 percent of my pay, around £700 a month, and I'd try to move into a role with customers, like advice. And I'd join the union rep team my mum is in, so I'm part of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year one. Five years feels like the length of a degree, which I know how to survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trust my mum, honestly, and a couple of seniors at Calder who've been through two recessions. I'd distrust any boss who says there's nothing to worry about. People in charge say that right before the cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to guide you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year picture I'm trying to hold on. Here I'm trying to land somewhere. I think I could be a good adviser for people who are scared of money, because I've learned to read files and listen at the same time.

say: I'd say we have a **window** and should use it for retraining and fair rules.
I'd talk about it on my local **forum** to help shape things.
think: I think I get about **five working years**, enough to build a base.
By 2031 anything I'm good at, a machine will do better, so it's **preparation**.
do: Finish my **exams**, then learn AI properly in work time.
Save around **£700** a month, close to 40 percent of pay.
Move toward an **advice** role with customers, and join the union.
feel: I feel **steadier** than with two years, like the length of a degree.
S3.quote: In the two-year picture I'm trying to hold on. Here I'm trying to land somewhere.
fieldNote: Five years changes his stance from **holding on** to landing somewhere.
He names advising as a **human-facing** niche, built on listening skills.
He is wary of **bosses** who say nothing will change.

steps.text: Finish the mortgage-advice qualifications by next summer
Use work time to learn the AI tools properly
Save £700 a month toward a safety fund
Join the union rep team my mum is in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time to do this right, with rules and retraining ready, and not wait for a crisis. I'd also say firms should start sharing the gains early, like shorter weeks. At work I'd say it with a smile, because it's not a threat to anyone yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a decade means I'll probably have a whole first career in finance, then a second one. I'd be thirty-two, maybe with a partner and a flat. It might even be exciting, as long as there's a safety net for people who didn't get a head start like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing in the job and take the advice exams. I'd save for a flat, maybe buy at around twenty-six. In year three I'd be an adviser or an underwriter, and I'd run a monthly AI workshop for newer staff, because teaching it makes me learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A decade is a long time and I'm not sitting on a ticking clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What would you be doing in year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By year three I'd have my advice licence and be speaking to customers face to face about their mortgages. I'd also be a staff rep, helping people handle the new tools. And I'd be living in my own flat, I hope, not paying someone else's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the long wait cost you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cost is that people don't act when it's far away. I've seen it with my mum's hospital: they knew the new system was coming and still weren't ready. I'd be one of the people pushing for early action, which is tiring but worth it.

say: I'd say a decade is enough to do this **right**, with rules and retraining ready.
I'd argue firms should share the **gains** early, like shorter weeks.
think: I think I get a whole first **career** in finance, then a second.
It could be **exciting** if there's a safety net for people without my head start.
do: Take the advice **exams** and aim for an adviser role.
Save for a **flat** and buy around age twenty-six.
Run a monthly **AI workshop** for newer staff.
feel: I feel **fairly calm**, because ten years is not a ticking clock.
S4.quote: I've seen it with my mum's hospital: they knew the new system was coming and still weren't ready.
fieldNote: With ten years Yusuf is **calm** and plans a staged career.
He wants to **teach** AI skills, a sign of his steady-adopter style.
He worries about **others** without his head start, a progressive habit.

steps.text: Pass the advice exams and move into an adviser role
Buy a small flat around age twenty-six
Run a monthly workshop on AI tools for new staff
Push for early rules on sharing the gains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because everything has to happen at once and I only have six months of savings. What would help is a clear guaranteed income, retraining paid for by the society, and the union at the table. I'd also want to know sooner rather than later what my employer plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I feel lucky, but not safe. Having a family that can back me up is a big advantage, and I'd like everyone to have something like it.

headlineQuote: I feel lucky, but not safe. Having a family that can back me up is a big advantage, and I'd like everyone to have something like it.
portrait: Yusuf, 22, is a **junior loan analyst** at a building society in Manchester, who uses AI tools sparingly and checks them.
His mum is a nurse and **union rep**, so he speaks up early and trusts collective action.
He thinks his first-pass checking work is **exposed**, and aims for advice and judgement roles.
Mood runs from calm in the plateau to **alarmed** at two years, then back to calm with ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because everything has to happen at once with six months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **income** and retraining paid for by his employer.
The **union** at the table and early news of the society's plans.
